prompt: How does the section describe the division between inorganic and organic chemistry today?

choices.text: It has become blurred: clear divisions between the two don't exist
It is sharp: every compound is one or the other, depending on whether it contains carbon
choices.why: Organometallic compounds contain both metals and carbon, so they can't be defined as only organic or only inorganic.

choices.text: It has disappeared, so the two are now a single field
choices.why: Both fields still exist. What's blurred is the boundary between them.

choices.text: It was fixed by the first issue of the journal Inorganic Chemistry
choices.why: No such ruling exists. Clear divisions don't exist, and the section expects more and more molecules that don't fit the traditional disciplines.

explanation: The division between inorganic and organic chemistry has become blurred. Organometallic compounds, which contain both metals and carbon, illustrate that clear divisions between the two fields don't exist.

prompt: What do all organometallic compounds contain?

choices.text: Metals bonded to carbon or to carbon-containing molecules
Metals bonded only to other metals
choices.why: The "organo" part matters: in organometallic compounds the metal is bonded to carbon or carbon-containing molecules.

choices.text: Carbon, but no metal
choices.why: A compound with carbon and no metal isn't organometallic. Organometallic compounds have metals bonded to carbon.

choices.text: Metal ions dissolved in water
choices.why: Dissolving a metal ion in water doesn't bond it to carbon. Organometallic compounds have metals bonded to carbon or carbon-containing molecules.

explanation: Organometallic compounds contain metals that are bonded to carbon or carbon-containing molecules.

prompt: Organometallic catalysts are one of the major classes of catalysts used for what?

choices.text: Organic synthesis reactions
Extracting metals from their ores
choices.why: Extracting metals is metallurgy. The section's example is organic synthesis: organometallic catalysts are a major class of catalysts for it.

choices.text: Making alloys such as bronze
choices.why: Bronze is made by mixing other elements with copper, with no catalyst involved. Organometallic catalysts are used for organic synthesis reactions.

choices.text: Conducting electricity in wires
choices.why: A catalyst speeds up a reaction; carrying a current is a different job. Organometallic catalysts are used for organic synthesis reactions.

explanation: One of the major classes of catalysts used for organic synthesis reactions is the organometallic catalysts, compounds that contain metals bonded to carbon or carbon-containing molecules.

prompt: Why are organometallic catalysts hard to classify as only organic or only inorganic?

choices.text: They contain metals, traditionally inorganic, and carbon, traditionally organic
They can't be made in a laboratory
choices.why: Where a compound comes from doesn't settle the question. The puzzle is that they contain both metals and carbon.

choices.text: They are found only in living things
choices.why: Many are catalysts for organic synthesis, not biological molecules. The puzzle is that they contain both metals and carbon.

choices.text: They contain neither carbon nor metals
choices.why: The opposite: organometallic compounds contain both, with metals bonded to carbon.

explanation: Are organometallic compounds inorganic because they contain metals, or organic because they contain carbon? They can't be defined as only one or the other, which illustrates that clear divisions between the two fields don't exist.

prompt: Why is it incorrect to class metals as "inorganic" in the sense of non-living or non-biological?

choices.text: Metal ions are common in biology
Metals always contain carbon
choices.why: Metals are elements in their own right. The reason is that metal ions are common in living things.

choices.text: Living things contain no carbon
choices.why: Living things are full of carbon-based molecules. The reason is that metal ions are common in biology too.

choices.text: Metals are never found in minerals
choices.why: Metals are found in minerals and ores. The point is that they're also common in biology.

explanation: Metal ions are common in biology, so the idea that metals are "inorganic" and thus non-living or non-biological is incorrect. The cobalt cofactor adenosylcobalamin is the canonical example.

prompt: Adenosylcobalamin is an important biological cofactor. Which metal ion does it contain?

choices.text: Cobalt (Co)
Copper (Cu)
choices.why: Watch the symbols: Cu is copper, Co is cobalt. Adenosylcobalamin contains a cobalt ion, with a cobalt–carbon bond.

choices.text: Iron (Fe)
choices.why: Adenosylcobalamin contains cobalt, not iron; the "cobal" in its name is a clue.

choices.text: Calcium (Ca)
choices.why: Adenosylcobalamin contains a cobalt ion, bonded to carbon, not calcium.

explanation: Adenosylcobalamin is an important biological cofactor containing a cobalt (Co) ion and a cobalt–carbon bond.

prompt: What makes adenosylcobalamin an organometallic compound?

choices.text: It has a cobalt–carbon bond
It is found in living things
choices.why: Being biological doesn't make a compound organometallic. What matters is a metal bonded to carbon, here the cobalt–carbon bond.

choices.text: It contains a cobalt ion
choices.why: Containing a metal isn't enough: in an organometallic compound the metal is bonded to carbon, as in adenosylcobalamin's cobalt–carbon bond.

choices.text: It acts as a catalyst
choices.why: Catalysts come in many kinds. Organometallic describes the bonding: a metal bonded to carbon, here cobalt to carbon.

explanation: Organometallic compounds contain metals bonded to carbon or carbon-containing molecules. Adenosylcobalamin contains a cobalt ion with a cobalt–carbon bond, so it is an organometallic catalyst that occurs in biology.

prompt: What does adenosylcobalamin illustrate about metals?

choices.text: "Inorganic" metals are important cofactors in biology
Only synthetic, laboratory catalysts contain metals
choices.why: Adenosylcobalamin is a natural biological cofactor, and it contains a cobalt ion.

choices.text: Biological molecules never contain metal–carbon bonds
choices.why: Adenosylcobalamin is a biological molecule with a cobalt–carbon bond.

choices.text: Metals belong only to the chemistry of non-living things
choices.why: That's the historical idea adenosylcobalamin shows to be wrong: metal ions are common in biology.

explanation: Adenosylcobalamin is an organometallic catalyst present in biology, illustrating that "inorganic" metals are important cofactors in biology and that metals aren't simply non-living or non-biological.

prompt: Some sub-fields of inorganic chemistry focus on the electrical conductivity of inorganic materials. Which three kinds of conductivity does the section name?

choices.text: Conduction, superconduction, and semiconduction
Conduction, convection, and radiation
choices.why: Convection and radiation are ways heat travels, not kinds of electrical conductivity. The section names conduction, superconduction, and semiconduction.

choices.text: Insulation, resistance, and conduction
choices.why: The section names conduction, superconduction, and semiconduction as the focus of these sub-fields.

explanation: Some sub-fields of inorganic chemistry focus on the electrical conductivity of inorganic materials (conduction, superconduction, and semiconduction), and others on the optical and electronic properties of inorganic nanomaterials.

choices.text: Through their extended conjugated π systems
Through metal atoms trapped inside them
choices.why: Carbon nanotubes are an allotrope of carbon. They conduct through their extended conjugated π systems, not through metal atoms.

choices.text: Through ions dissolved in them
choices.why: Nanotubes conduct through the electrons of their extended conjugated π systems, not through dissolved ions.

choices.text: They can't: only metals conduct electricity
choices.why: Electrical conductivity is a canonical property of metals, but carbon-based materials such as nanotubes also conduct.

explanation: Electrical conductivity is a canonical property of metals, but carbon-based materials also conduct: carbon nanotubes conduct electricity through their extended conjugated π systems.

prompt: Buckminsterfullerene, the most famous fullerene, has the formula C60. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of it?
explanation: The subscript in C60 gives the number of carbon atoms: 60. Buckminsterfullerene, or the "buckyball", is made of carbon alone.

prompt: According to the section, when can fullerenes demonstrate superconductivity?

choices.text: When they are combined with metals and crystallized
As single, isolated molecules
choices.why: The section says fullerenes show superconductivity when combined with metals and crystallized, not as isolated molecules.

choices.text: When they are dissolved in water
choices.why: The section's condition is combining fullerenes with metals and crystallizing them.

choices.text: Never: superconductivity is only found in pure metals
choices.why: Fullerenes combined with metals and crystallized can demonstrate superconductivity.

explanation: Fullerenes such as Buckminsterfullerene (C60) have interesting properties similar to nanoparticles, and when combined with metals and crystallized they can demonstrate superconductivity.

prompt: Carbon nanotubes and fullerenes are made of carbon alone. Why have inorganic chemists embraced them as "inorganic"?

choices.text: They behave more like inorganic materials than like smaller organic molecules
They contain metal atoms
choices.why: Nanotubes and fullerenes are allotropes of carbon, with no metal in them. It's their behavior that is familiar to inorganic chemists.

choices.text: They are mined from minerals
choices.why: Where they come from isn't the reason. Inorganic chemists claim them because their properties resemble those of inorganic materials.

choices.text: Organic chemists showed that they aren't carbon compounds
choices.why: They are allotropes of carbon. They count as "inorganic" because of how they behave, not what they're made of.

explanation: Although carbon nanotubes and fullerenes are allotropes of carbon, their material properties are familiar to inorganic chemists, who have embraced them as "inorganic" because they behave more like inorganic materials than smaller organic molecules.

prompt: Why are the material properties of carbon nanotubes and fullerenes somewhat foreign to many organic chemists?

choices.text: Organic chemists have traditionally focused on smaller organic molecules with very different properties
They contain elements that organic chemists don't study
choices.why: Nanotubes and fullerenes are made only of carbon. It's their unusual material properties that are foreign.

choices.text: They are too reactive to handle
choices.why: The section's reason is about familiarity: organic chemists traditionally studied smaller molecules with very different properties.

choices.text: Organic chemists aren't allowed to study materials
choices.why: Nothing forbids it. These materials are simply unlike the smaller organic molecules that organic chemists traditionally focused on.

explanation: Organic chemists have traditionally focused on smaller organic molecules with very different properties, so the material properties of carbon nanotubes and fullerenes are somewhat foreign to them, but familiar to inorganic chemists.

prompt: What does the section expect the future to hold for the classification of molecules?

choices.text: More and more molecules that don't fit into the traditional disciplines of chemistry
A strict new boundary between organic and inorganic chemistry
choices.why: The section expects the boundary to blur further, with more and more molecules that don't fit the traditional disciplines.

choices.text: Organic chemistry taking over all carbon-based materials
choices.why: The trend runs the other way: inorganic chemists have already embraced carbon materials such as nanotubes and fullerenes.

explanation: Carbon nanotubes, fullerenes, and organometallic compounds already don't fit neatly into "organic" or "inorganic", and the section says the future will certainly hold more and more examples of molecules that don't fit the traditional disciplines.
